body:
How computers represent information

A computer can store and process many kinds of information, including numbers, written text, photographs, audio recordings and videos. Although these appear very different to the user, a digital computer represents them internally using combinations of just 2 symbols: 0 and 1.

These symbols are called binary digits. The word binary means that the system uses 2 possible values. In digital electronic systems, these values can represent 2 distinguishable states, such as low and high electrical signals.

The meaning of a particular sequence of binary digits depends on how it is interpreted. The same sequence may represent a number, part of a letter, an image value or another kind of information.

Bit: A bit, short for binary digit, is the basic unit of digital information. It has 2 possible values: 0 or 1.

Bits, nibbles and bytes

A single bit can distinguish only 2 possibilities. Combining several bits allows a computer to represent more possibilities.

  • 1 bit: 1 binary digit, either 0 or 1.
  • 1 nibble: A group of 4 bits.
  • 1 byte: A group of 8 bits, equivalent to 2 nibbles.

For example, 1010 is a 4-bit sequence, while 10100110 is an 8-bit sequence. If each bit has 2 possible values, a group of 4 bits has 24 = 16 possible combinations. A group of 8 bits has 28 = 256 possible combinations.

When interpreted as an unsigned whole number, 1 byte can therefore represent any integer from 0 through 255. This does not mean that every byte in a computer represents a number or that every character always occupies exactly 1 byte.

Decimal and binary number systems

The decimal number system, used in everyday counting, has base 10 and uses the digits 0 through 9. The binary number system has base 2 and uses only 0 and 1.

Both are positional number systems. The value of a digit depends on its position. In decimal, positions from right to left have values 1, 10, 100 and 1,000. In binary, they have values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.

Each binary position is therefore worth twice as much as the position immediately to its right.

Converting a binary number into decimal

Consider the binary number 1011. Its digits occupy positions worth 8, 4, 2 and 1, beginning from the left.

10112 = (1 × 8) + (0 × 4) + (1 × 2) + (1 × 1) = 1110.

The subscript 2 identifies a binary number, while the subscript 10 identifies a decimal number.

Similarly, 10102 = 8 + 2 = 1010. The written sequence 10 has different values depending on its base: 102 equals 210.

Adding zeros to the left of a positive binary integer does not change its numerical value. For example, 001012 and 1012 both represent decimal 5.

Converting a decimal number into binary

To represent a non-negative decimal integer in binary, express it as a sum of powers of 2. For example, decimal 13 equals 8 + 4 + 1. Therefore, the binary positions worth 8, 4 and 1 contain 1, while the position worth 2 contains 0.

Thus, 1310 = 11012.

Why binary representation matters

Binary representation provides the common foundation for digital information. Numbers can be written in binary, while letters and symbols can be assigned numeric codes that are represented using bits. Images and sounds are also converted into digital data according to their respective representations.

Binary is a number system and a method of representing digital information; it is not itself a document, image or audio file format. File formats determine how groups of bits are organised and interpreted.

Prelims focus

  • Binary is a base-2 number system using 0 and 1.
  • Decimal is a base-10 number system using digits 0 through 9.
  • 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits.
  • 4 bits allow 16 combinations; 8 bits allow 256 combinations.
  • 10102 = 1010; 10112 = 1110.
  • Trap: 102 is decimal 2, not decimal 10.

[Sources: National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS), Computer Science (330), Lesson 1, Computer Fundamentals, §1.6, printed pp. 12–13; NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Chapter 1, Computer System, §1.3.1, and Chapter 2, Encoding Schemes and Number System, §§2.1–2.3, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 14 November 2026.]

title: Digital Information: Bits, Bytes and the Binary Number System

body:
Why computers need different kinds of memory

A computer must keep information available while it processes instructions. Some information is needed immediately, while other information may be required only occasionally or must remain available for future use.

No single type of memory provides the highest speed, largest capacity and lowest cost simultaneously. Computer systems therefore use different memory and storage components for different purposes.

The arrangement of these components according to their usual access speed, capacity and relationship with the processor is called the memory hierarchy.

Understanding the memory hierarchy

For a conventional computer, a useful simplified order from faster to slower access is:

  1. Registers: Very small storage locations inside the central processing unit (CPU) that hold information currently being used in processing.
  2. Cache memory: Small, high-speed memory that keeps frequently or recently needed data and instructions close to the processor.
  3. Random Access Memory (RAM): Main working memory that holds the data and instructions of active applications.
  4. Secondary storage: Devices such as solid-state drives and hard disk drives that retain files and other information for future use.

Moving down this simplified hierarchy, access generally becomes slower, available capacity generally increases and cost per unit of storage generally decreases. Actual speed and capacity depend on the system and device.

Registers and cache memory

Registers

Registers are small storage locations within the CPU. They hold data, instructions or intermediate results needed directly during processing. They are typically the fastest and smallest level in the hierarchy.

Cache memory

Cache memory reduces the time required for the CPU to obtain information from slower main memory. It holds copies of selected data and instructions that may be needed again.

When required information is available in the cache, the processor can use it without waiting for the same information to be retrieved from RAM. If it is not available in the cache, the processor must obtain it from a lower level of memory.

Cache is generally faster than RAM but has much smaller capacity. Its purpose is to improve the speed of accessing information, not to provide large, permanent file storage.

Random Access Memory: the working memory

RAM stands for Random Access Memory. It is the main working memory used while a computer is operating. Programs and data needed for active tasks are loaded into RAM so the processor can access them efficiently.

For example, when a user opens a document saved on a storage drive, the computer loads the information needed for viewing and editing into working memory. Changes made during the session may exist in RAM before they are saved to permanent storage.

Conventional RAM is volatile memory. This means it requires power to retain its contents. When power is removed, the information held in RAM is lost.

RAM is normally read-write memory: data can be retrieved from it and changed during normal computer operation.

RAM is not the same as permanent storage. A document that is merely open in an application is not necessarily saved. Unsaved changes may disappear if power is lost, even though an earlier saved version remains on the storage drive.

Read Only Memory: retaining essential instructions

ROM stands for Read Only Memory. Unlike conventional RAM, it is non-volatile, meaning its contents remain available when power is switched off.

ROM and related non-volatile firmware memory are used to retain essential instructions needed during the computer's startup process. These instructions help initialise the system before the operating system is loaded.

Although the name means read-only memory, some technologies used for firmware allow contents to be updated through special procedures. Therefore, the essential distinction for basic computer knowledge is that ROM retains its stored information without continuous power, whereas conventional RAM does not.

RAM and ROM compared

FeatureRAMROM
Full formRandom Access MemoryRead Only Memory
VolatilityVolatileNon-volatile
Main purposeActive programs and working dataRetaining essential instructions or firmware
Normal operationFrequently read and writtenUsually read; updating depends on technology
After power removalContents are lostContents are retained

Primary memory and secondary storage

In basic computer classification, RAM and ROM are commonly identified as types of primary memory. Cache and registers are additional high-speed memory levels associated closely with processing.

Secondary storage has a different purpose: retaining larger amounts of information, such as documents, photographs and applications, for future use. Common examples are HDDs, SSDs, memory cards and optical discs.

A useful distinction is that primary working memory supports current processing, while secondary storage preserves information beyond the current session.

Prelims focus

  • Registers are very small, high-speed storage locations within the CPU.
  • Cache reduces the average time needed to access frequently used information.
  • RAM is volatile and is used as main working memory.
  • ROM is non-volatile and is associated with stored startup instructions or firmware.
  • SSD and HDD are secondary storage devices, not forms of RAM.
  • Trap: Not all primary memory is volatile; ROM is non-volatile.

[Sources: NIOS, Computer Science (330), Lesson 1, Computer Fundamentals, §1.4.3, printed p. 6, and §§1.6.1–1.6.3, printed pp. 13–15; NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Chapter 1, Computer System, §1.3.2, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: From registers to secondary storage, access slows as capacity grows; ROM retains startup firmware when power is off.
pictures.caption: The memory hierarchy balances fast access near the CPU with larger, persistent storage.

title: Computer Memory Hierarchy: Registers, Cache, RAM and ROM

body:
Why secondary storage is necessary

Computer users need to preserve documents, photographs, applications and other files after a computer has been switched off. Conventional RAM cannot perform this function by itself because it is volatile.

Secondary storage, also called auxiliary storage, provides non-volatile storage for information that must remain available for later use.

Secondary storage generally offers larger capacity at a lower cost per unit of data than high-speed working memory. It is usually slower than RAM, but it is designed to retain information independently of the computer's normal processing session.

A secondary storage device may be installed inside a computer or connected externally. Whether the device is internal or external does not determine whether it is primary or secondary storage.

Magnetic storage devices

Hard Disk Drive

A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores digital information magnetically on rotating platters. It uses a mechanical mechanism to read and write data.

HDDs are commonly used for storing applications, documents, photographs, videos and backups. They can provide substantial storage capacity at a comparatively low cost.

Because a traditional HDD has moving mechanical components, reading data involves mechanical activity. This helps explain why HDDs generally have slower access times than modern solid-state drives.

Magnetic tape

Magnetic tape also uses magnetic material to store data. Information is recorded along a tape rather than on a rotating hard disk platter.

Tape is useful for storing large collections of data and long-term backups. Access is generally sequential, so locating a particular item may take longer than on a disk.

Both HDDs and magnetic tapes belong to the magnetic storage category.

Optical storage devices

Optical storage uses laser-based technology to read information recorded on a disc. Common examples include Compact Discs (CDs) and Digital Versatile Discs (DVDs).

A DVD typically holds more information than a standard CD of the corresponding basic type.

Optical discs can differ in whether their information may be changed:

  • CD-ROM: A read-only disc whose recorded contents are not intended to be modified.
  • CD-R: A recordable disc designed for writing data without ordinary rewriting of previously recorded data.
  • CD-RW: A rewritable disc that allows recorded information to be erased and rewritten.

These distinctions concern the recording capability of an optical disc, not the difference between RAM and ROM inside a computer.

Solid-state and flash-based storage

Solid-state storage stores information electronically without relying on rotating magnetic platters for reading and writing.

Common examples include:

  • Solid-State Drive (SSD): A non-volatile storage drive commonly used for operating systems, applications and personal files.
  • USB flash drive or pen drive: Portable flash-based storage used for transferring and carrying files.
  • SD and microSD memory cards: Small flash storage media commonly used in cameras, phones and other compatible devices.

An SSD generally offers faster access and has no moving mechanical read-write parts, unlike a traditional HDD. The relative performance of particular devices nevertheless depends on their design and connection.

A USB connection does not itself identify the storage technology. For example, an external HDD and a USB flash drive may both connect through USB, even though one uses magnetic storage and the other uses flash memory.

Saving and transferring files

Suppose a user saves a document to a USB flash drive. The document becomes stored as non-volatile digital information on the drive. The drive can then be disconnected safely and used with another compatible device to access the saved file.

Different devices may use different storage technologies, but they can store many of the same file formats. A PDF document, for example, may be kept on an HDD, SSD, USB flash drive or memory card.

Cloud storage

Cloud storage allows files to be stored on remote computer systems and accessed through a network service. The underlying data are still held on physical storage devices operated by the service provider.

Cloud storage is therefore a method of accessing and managing remotely stored information, not a separate physical recording technology comparable to magnetic or optical storage.

Some cloud services also keep synchronised copies on the user's device, allowing selected files to remain accessible without an active internet connection.

Choosing storage for different purposes

Storage technology is selected according to required capacity, speed, portability, cost and intended use. SSDs are useful when rapid access is important; HDDs provide economical high-capacity storage; flash drives and memory cards support portability; optical discs provide removable media; and magnetic tape remains useful for certain backup and archival purposes.

Keeping a separate backup copy is important because non-volatile storage retains information when power is removed but does not guarantee protection against device failure, accidental deletion or damage.

Prelims focus

  • HDD and magnetic tape use magnetic storage.
  • CD and DVD are optical storage media.
  • SSD, pen drives and SD cards use solid-state or flash-based storage.
  • Secondary storage is generally non-volatile.
  • CD-ROM is read-only; CD-R is recordable; CD-RW is rewritable.
  • Trap: An SSD and an HDD are both secondary storage devices, but they do not use the same recording technology.

[Sources: NIOS, Computer Science (330), Lesson 1, Computer Fundamentals, §1.6.3, printed pp. 15–18; NCERT, Computer Science, Class 11, Chapter 1, Computer System, §1.3.2, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 14 November 2026; Microsoft Support, What is Microsoft cloud storage?, section What is Microsoft cloud storage and what is my quota?, accessed 14 November 2026.]
